items.title: SessionStart hook injecting version-manager env into agent sessions
items.problem: Agent shells inherit a version-manager shim PATH with no resolved versions, so common interpreters fail inside Claude Code sessions.
items.you: No SessionStart hook. Bash tool calls hit asdf shims directly; a bare `python3` dies with 'No version is set for command python3' because this repo pins no python in .tool-versions at the repo root. Hit twice in this very session, forcing /usr/bin/python3 fallbacks.
items.them: settings.json SessionStart hook: `mise env -s zsh >> "$CLAUDE_ENV_FILE"` — the resolved runtime env is materialized into every session's environment before the first tool call.
items.difference: Not ergonomics. Every agent shell command that touches a managed runtime is a coin flip today, and the failure mode (shim error, not 'command not found') is confusing enough that the agent papers over it with absolute paths instead of fixing the root cause.
items.translation: Add a SessionStart hook to home/.claude/settings.json running `asdf env` equivalent (asdf has no `env` subcommand; export ASDF_DIR/ASDF_DATA_DIR and prepend the shims dir, or resolve `asdf where python` per tool) into $CLAUDE_ENV_FILE. Alternative, smaller: pin a python in home/.tool-versions so the shim always resolves.

items.title: Local desktop notification on agent Stop/Notification
items.problem: Long agent turns finish silently; you don't know when it's your turn.
items.you: `agentPushNotifEnabled: true` in settings.json — phone push only. Nothing on the machine you're sitting at.
items.them: claude/notify.sh wired to both Notification and Stop hooks, rendering a terminal notification with an icon; distinct title/body for 'all done — your turn' vs a permission prompt.
items.difference: Push-to-phone has multi-second latency and pulls attention off the machine. A local notification closes the loop where the work is.
items.translation: home/.claude/notify.sh (already covered by the home/.claude directory symlink in the manifest) using osascript or terminal-notifier on Darwin, plus a tmux display-message fallback since interactive shells auto-attach tmux. Wire Stop + Notification hooks in home/.claude/settings.json. Theirs is kitty-specific — ours must be iTerm/Terminal-safe.

items.title: Custom Claude Code statusline (context %, cache hit rate, cost, branch)
items.problem: No visibility into context pressure or spend during a session until it bites.
items.you: Default statusline. No statusLine key in home/.claude/settings.json.
items.them: claude/statusline.sh: model, effort, context-used % with green/yellow/red thresholds, prompt-cache hit rate, running cost, cwd, git branch.
items.difference: The cache-hit metric is the interesting one — it makes an invisible cost driver visible. Context % matters more here than for most: autoCompact behavior and a 1M-context model make it easy to drift without noticing.
items.translation: home/.claude/statusline.sh + statusLine key in home/.claude/settings.json. Needs jq (already in Brewfile? verify). Keep it bash, no color assumptions beyond ANSI.

items.title: Curl-able bootstrap script for a bare machine
items.problem: Getting from a fresh OS to a working checkout requires reading the README and typing.
items.you: README documents `xcode-select --install` then `git clone` then cd — you have to have the README open on a machine that has no browser config yet.
items.them: `curl -s https://dotfiles.<domain>/boot.sh | bash` — script/boot.sh installs git if missing, clones to ~/.dotfiles, and hands off to script/setup.sh. Published to GitHub Pages by a CI workflow that copies script/boot.sh into the Pages artifact, so the URL can never drift from the repo.
items.difference: One memorized string vs a document. Also makes the first two steps CI-testable instead of prose.
items.translation: scripts/boot.sh (git presence check → clone → exec the converge entry point). Skip the Pages hosting: `curl -sL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nonrational/dotfiles/main/scripts/boot.sh | bash` needs no domain or workflow. Add a CI step that shellchecks/dry-runs it.

items.title: Merge tracked settings onto a live file instead of skip-worktree
items.problem: Some tools rewrite their own settings.json in place, injecting machine-local or private values that must not reach a public repo — but the file also holds config you want tracked.
items.you: `git update-index --skip-worktree` on home/.gemini/antigravity-cli/settings.json, plus a documented three-step dance (make unskip-mutable-settings → stage everything except trustedWorkspaces → commit → re-skip) every time you want to change a tracked value.
items.them: bin/claude-setup: a Ruby script that deep-merges the repo's settings onto whatever is live — repo wins scalars, live-only keys survive, hook arrays are unioned — after snapshotting the live file to a timestamped backup. Idempotent, re-run whenever drift appears. The file is deliberately excluded from the symlink deploy.
items.difference: skip-worktree hides drift rather than reconciling it: git stops showing you the file, so a private path can sit in your working tree indefinitely and a stale flag silently swallows a real edit. A merge script makes the reconciliation explicit, re-runnable, and reviewable, and the backup makes a bad merge one `cp` from undone.
items.translation: scripts/reconcile-settings.sh (bash + jq, matching repo conventions — no Ruby dependency) driven by a small table of file → private-key-allowlist. Drop the manifest entry for the file, add `make reconcile-settings`, retire skip-mutable-settings/unskip-mutable-settings, update the CLAUDE.md gotcha. Must write a backup before touching anything.
items.spike_question: Can a jq-based reconcile merge the tracked keys of a tool-rewritten settings.json without ever staging a machine-local or private key, and does it stay correct when the tool rewrites the file while a session is live? If yes, what does it cost to retire skip-worktree on home/.gemini/antigravity-cli/settings.json?

items.title: Single namespaced CLI over the flat bin/ and make targets
items.problem: Personal tooling is discoverable only if you already remember its name.
items.you: Two disjoint surfaces: ~19 make targets (deploy, check-*, macos-*, link-*, backup-*) and 22 unrelated scripts in home/bin.Darwin (asdf-tidy, dns-kill, gh-tidy-repos, pgkill, speed-up...). No index, no help, no grouping. You find a tool by `ls ~/bin` and recognizing the name.
items.them: `robot` dispatches to `bin/<namespace>` scripts (theme, dotfiles, arch), each of which dispatches to `bin/<namespace>-<verb>`. Every level prints a colored usage listing when called bare. `robot dotfiles up`, `robot theme set`.
items.difference: One entry point you can type blind and get a menu from. The bin/<ns>-<verb> file convention means adding a subcommand is adding a file — no registry to update. Costs a second layer of indirection for scripts you already invoke directly.
items.translation: home/bin.Darwin/<name> as the dispatcher; group existing scripts by prefix (git-*, macos-*, brew-*) and have the dispatcher shell out to them and to make targets. Do NOT move the existing scripts — keep them directly invokable, make the dispatcher additive.
items.rationale: make targets plus a flat bin/ already work; a dispatcher adds a layer of indirection without adding a capability.

items.title: Codebase-audit git aliases (churn, bus-factor, hotspots, velocity)
items.problem: Answering 'what's risky in this repo' means writing the same log|sort|uniq pipelines from memory each time.
items.you: ~60 aliases in home/.gitconfig plus home/.githelpers, all workflow-oriented (branch management, wildcards, pretty logs). Nothing for repo forensics — grep for churn/bus-factor/hotspot/velocity returns nothing.
items.them: Five aliases under a `## Codebase Audit Commands` heading: churn (20 most-changed files in a year), bus-factor (shortlog -sn), bug-hotspots (files in fix/bug commits), commit-velocity (commits by month), firefighting (reverts/hotfixes in a year).
items.difference: Small, but these are exactly the questions you ask when landing in an unfamiliar repo, and each is a pipeline nobody remembers cold. Zero blast radius — pure addition.
items.translation: Add to home/.gitconfig under a commented section, or as functions in home/.githelpers if the pipelines get long (that file already exists for exactly this). Match the existing alias naming and comment style.
items.rationale: ~60 aliases and .githelpers already cover the daily workflow; repo forensics is rare enough to write ad hoc when it comes up.

items.title: ERR trap reporting failing command and source:line in repo scripts
items.problem: A `set -e` script that dies mid-run prints whatever the failing command printed and nothing about where it was.
items.you: deploy.sh runs `set -euf -o pipefail` with no ERR trap. A failure inside parse_manifest or the apply loop exits silently with the raw exit code; same for test/test_deploy.sh and test/test_shell.sh.
items.them: `trap on_script_error ERR` printing `Command '$BASH_COMMAND' failed at ${BASH_SOURCE[1]}:${BASH_LINENO[0]}` before re-raising the exit code.
items.difference: Turns 'the deploy exited 1' into 'line 84 of deploy.sh, this exact command'. Matters most for the scripts you run rarely and under pressure — bootstrap on a new machine, CI on a platform you're not sitting at.
items.translation: A few lines at the top of deploy.sh; if it earns a second caller, extract to scripts/lib/strict.sh and source it from deploy.sh and the two test scripts. Verify it doesn't fire on the intentional non-zero paths in audit mode.

items.title: Cross-app theme switching via a current/ symlink indirection
items.problem: Changing color scheme means editing N app configs, and per-machine theme choice can't be committed without hardcoding it for every machine.
items.you: Nothing. No theme management anywhere in the repo; terminal/editor colors are set per-app by hand.
items.them: etc/themes/<name>/ holds one file per app (kitty.conf, nvim.lua, btop.theme, alacritty.toml, background.png). `theme set` points ~/.config/dotfiles/current/theme at the chosen dir, relinks each app's config file at it, flips OS dark/light mode, sets the wallpaper, and signals running apps to reload. Interactive picker via gum when no arg.
items.difference: The `current/` indirection is the actual idea: app configs point at a stable path, so the machine-local choice is a symlink (never committed) while the themes themselves are tracked. Same trick that would let per-machine anything be selected without a per-host file.
items.translation: etc/themes/<name>/ + a switcher script; ~/.config/dotfiles/current/theme as the indirection point. Applies to far less here — bash + tmux + iTerm/Terminal, not a tiling-WM stack — so the payoff is tmux.conf colors, vim, and macOS appearance, and iTerm profiles resist file-level theming.
items.rationale: built for a tiling-WM stack this machine does not have; iTerm profiles resist file-level theming, so the payoff is tmux and vim colors only.

items.title: One idempotent converge command replacing the README's manual sequence
items.problem: Bringing a machine to desired state — new or existing — requires executing a documented sequence by hand, in order, and knowing which steps to skip on a re-run.
items.you: README carries a ~15-step shell block: xcode-select, clone, make brew-install, make brew-bundle, chsh, restart terminal, make init-submodules, make deploy, make link-karabiner, gh auth login, make link-sublime, make restore-preferences, restart iTerm, make macos-reset-dock, make macos-disable-restore-apps-on-login, make macos. No single entry point, and prose is the only thing encoding the ordering constraints.
items.them: script/setup.sh is THE command — for install and for updates alike ('From there, use ./script/setup.sh to apply updates'). It sources an OS-specific script, links dotfiles, reconciles agent config, installs pinned global runtimes, sets the theme, installs gh extensions. Every function is idempotent, so re-running is the normal case.
items.difference: Ordering constraints live in code, not prose, so they can't rot silently and CI can exercise them. Turns 'set up a new machine' and 'catch this machine up after 3 months' into the same command. The real cost is that some steps genuinely aren't idempotent here (chsh, terminal restarts, macOS reboots) and pretending otherwise makes the script lie.
items.translation: scripts/setup.sh sourcing scripts/setup_darwin.sh / setup_linux.sh, calling the existing make targets in order. Interactive/reboot-requiring steps become explicit checkpoints that print and exit rather than steps that silently no-op. README shrinks to one command plus the checkpoint list. CI already runs deploy apply+audit against a temp $HOME — extend it to run the converge script's non-privileged path.
items.pilot: scripts/setup.sh covering only the steps that are already safely idempotent — init-submodules, deploy, brew-bundle, check-symlinks — and printing the remaining manual steps as a numbered checklist. README keeps the full block until the script covers it. Rollback: delete the script; nothing else changed.
items.spike_question: Which of the README's ~15 setup steps are genuinely idempotent, and can the ones that are not (chsh, terminal restart, macOS reboot, gh auth login) be expressed as checkpoints that print and halt rather than steps that silently no-op? If the checkpoint set is small, the converge script is honest; if it is most of the list, it is a lie with a shell wrapper.

items.title: Replace bespoke manifest+deploy.sh with rcm (rcup/lsrc, tags)
items.problem: Symlinking a tree into $HOME with OS/host conditionals is a solved problem with an off-the-shelf tool.
items.you: manifest (3 columns: source, target, condition) + deploy.sh (~apply/audit/--dry-run, bash, symlink-only by design). 31 explicit manifest lines, one per target. Tested by test/test_deploy.sh against a temp $HOME, exercised in CI on macOS and ubuntu.
items.them: rcm: `rcup -fv -x <excludes> -S <symlink-whole-dir> -t <tag>` with tag-<name>/ directories overlaying the base tree, tag resolved from uname/os-release. No per-file declaration — the file tree IS the manifest. lsrc previews what would link.
items.difference: rcm removes ~200 lines of bash and its test suite in exchange for a Homebrew dependency and convention-over-configuration. But the explicit manifest is doing real work here that tags can't: per-tool conditions (tool=git-town), per-host lines (host=nyx), and renames (home/bin.Darwin → ~/bin). rcm's tag model is a strictly weaker version of the condition column.
items.translation: Would mean restructuring home/ into base + tag-darwin/ + tag-linux/, encoding tool= and host= conditions some other way, deleting deploy.sh and test/test_deploy.sh, and adding rcm to Brewfile as a bootstrap prerequisite.
items.pilot: Not worth piloting unless the benefit is nameable — see spike_question.
items.rationale: rcm's tag model is strictly weaker than the manifest's condition column (cannot express tool=, host=, or the bin.Darwin -> ~/bin rename), and manifest-deploy already shipped.

items.title: fish as the interactive shell (sibling to the zsh-migration spike)
items.problem: Bash gives weak out-of-the-box interactive ergonomics: no autosuggestions, no syntax highlighting, completions only where someone wrote them.
items.you: bash-first by design (Homebrew bash via chsh). ~257 lines across .bashrc/.bashrc.Darwin/.bashrc.Linux/.bashrc.nyx/.bash_profile/.profile, a .bash_completion.d tree, ~90 lines of secondary zsh, and 11 bash scripts in bin.Darwin. .githelpers is bash functions sourced by git aliases.
items.them: config/fish (~169 lines: config.fish, conf.d/exports.fish, conf.d/aliases.fish, functions/, completions/) alongside a maintained bash and zsh, with ~/.config/fish/local.fish as the untracked escape hatch. starship supplies the prompt across all three, so the prompt is not shell-specific.
items.difference: fish gets autosuggestions, syntax highlighting, and generated completions with zero plugin management, where zsh needs a framework or hand-wired plugins. The price is non-POSIX syntax: the rc files cannot be shared, and every conditional and function in the existing 257 lines is a rewrite, not a port. Their setup sidesteps this by maintaining all three shells in parallel rather than migrating.
items.translation: home/.config/fish/ plus manifest entries; the OS/host branching would move from .bashrc.<platform>/.bashrc.<host> filename suffixes to conf.d/ files. The tmux auto-attach block at the end of .bashrc.Darwin and its guards (CLAUDECODE/AI_AGENT markers, TERM_PROGRAM allowlist) would need a fish equivalent. Scripts and git aliases stay bash regardless.
items.pilot: Install fish and run it as a non-login shell for a week without chsh, porting only exports and aliases. Nothing in the repo changes until the week is up.
items.spike_question: Do fish's out-of-the-box interactive ergonomics beat zsh-plus-plugins or ble.sh-on-bash by enough to justify a non-POSIX rc language, given ~257 lines of bash rc that cannot be ported mechanically and a bash-first deploy? Compare all three against the same concrete list of daily interactions, and decide against zsh-migration (#9) rather than in isolation.
